title: Dr. Steve Traynelis:
headline: In 2011 two children changed his research. Fifteen years on he explains why progress is slow, and why that slow road still leads somewhere.
story: Dr. Traynelis opens on a question: were these the only two kids on the planet? In 2011 NIH sent him two patients with GRIN variants, and his decades of lab work found a new purpose. Then the honest part: why research is slow, and why seeing the families brings it home.

He ends with what a family can do today (join the registries) and with balanced hope: “they're coming, but they're not going to be here tomorrow.” It must feel honest and hopeful. Never a date for a cure.

Never say or show that GRIN disorders can be prevented, are anyone's fault, or have a cure soon.
No shots of people eating. No childcare-room shots unless Nick confirms consent.
Do not reuse a B-roll shot that another researcher film uses.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of MVI_0936.MP4 (Interview 4). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Labels are automatic and often wrong. The transcript spells his name "Treneles": it is Traynelis.
[00:24] I'm a professor at Emory University, and I've been there since 1994.
[00:29] All of my research for, since 1985, has involved a neurotransmitter system in the brain called the glutamate system.
[00:39] And glutamate mediates excitatory synaptic transmission.
[00:43] We worked on everything you could imagine related to this system, animals, circuits, molecules, biophysics.
[00:50] And in 2011, I got contacted by the Undiagnosed Disease Program at NIH.
[00:55] They were sequencing kids really for the first time, really all patients, and they had these variants,
[01:02] grin mutations in two patients, and asked me, you want to work on those?
[01:06] And so, long story short, we did experiments on synthetic DNA and found profound changes,
[01:14] and that sort of set us on a path to figure out how prevalent this was.
[01:20] Was it super rare? Were these the only two kids on the planet?
[01:23] Or, in fact, were there a ton of these kids and nobody realized it?
[01:28] And we continue to work.
[01:29] But that's the entrée, and so my role has been in the capacity of understanding at the protein level,
[01:36] in these receptors I've worked on for decades, what happens when one amino acid or several amino acids get changed.
[01:46] Interviewer: So why is it important or matter for science and families to come together in a single event?
[01:54] So there's many reasons.
[01:56] That's an easy question to answer in the sense that there's so many good things that come out of it.
[02:02] Families need hope.
[02:03] They need to know that there are folks out there who not only have sympathy for what they're going through,
[02:11] have empathy for where they are in the process, but are actively working to solve problems.
[02:16] And the researchers need to know that their work actually impacts real people.
[02:23] And the latter might seem possibly unnecessary because all of us chose science to help others,
[02:30] but when you're in a laboratory all day and you're fighting bureaucracy and struggling to pay your people
[02:34] and get your experiments to work and fix your broken equipment,
[02:37] you sometimes lose sight of the fact that what you're doing actually has tangible outcome today on people.
[02:43] Everything seems far away.
[02:46] Someday maybe somebody will use what I learned.
[02:48] And so seeing the families, seeing the kids, brings it home.
[02:52] It's motivational, and particularly for the young people, it energizes them,
[02:56] and they begin to realize that this is a career that I can't just be proud of and feel like I'm doing something.
[03:04] It's a career that actually, tangibly, is doing something.
[03:22] I think the best hope would be for them to gain a balanced view of where we are
[03:31] without swinging too far to the side of despair.
[03:36] This is how it's always going to be. Nothing's ever coming from this.
[03:39] I just got to suck it up and plow through.
[03:44] And on the converse, we wouldn't want them to swing to the side of exuberant, irrational hope
[03:53] that maybe next month there's going to be a cure.
[03:56] There has to be a balance.
[03:58] There's hope. There's things in the pipeline. They'll take time.
[04:01] They may impact their kids' life.
[04:04] It might be a couple years. It might be a decade.
[04:07] But they're coming, but they're not going to be here tomorrow.
[04:11] It's not like at the next meeting we're going to disband because it's done.
[04:16] And I think if they have that balance, it just makes it easier to live their life,
[04:20] and it can buffer the ups and downs.
[04:40] The conferences are absolutely essential.
[04:41] Person-to-person contact is irreplaceable.
[04:44] Incidental conversations drive interesting ideas.
[05:54] I would encourage everybody to come.
[05:56] The parents should come to at least one or more.
[06:10] I think all the parents would benefit from knowing a part of the community
[06:15] and seeing a larger group of folks working on their problem.
[06:20] I think the scientists would go for the reasons I mentioned earlier.
[06:23] It's energizing. It's motivating.
[06:38] I think one thing that would be great, I know Simon's Foundation does this,
[06:43] and different organizations do it to different capacity depending on their resources,
[06:48] but what would be great is fund students, postdocs, young people.
[06:54] Get them here. Get them seeing folks in need
[06:58] and help them understand their career path has benefit, has potential.
[07:43] Interviewer: how you're working every day and the progress is just slow in science.
[07:49] One of the reasons research is so slow is the problems are hard.
[07:53] Biology is incredibly complex.
[07:56] I used to think I was a physical scientist,
[07:58] and I thought atoms and subatomic particles were more complicated by biology than biology,
[08:03] but a decade ago I flipped it around.
[08:07] We just scratched the surface,
[08:08] and these problems produced by these grid invariants go many layers deep,
[08:15] and sometimes we don't even know what the right experiment to do is.
[08:20] It just takes a long time to conceptualize the right way to do things,
[08:23] to redo them, figure out if what you identified is correct,
[08:29] talk to your colleagues, make sure they reproduce it.
[08:31] The whole scientific process is a slow one.
[08:35] Some of the methods and techniques,
[08:38] we fight with our equipment, it breaks, we have to fix it,
[08:41] we get weird noise, problems that need to be sorted out.
[08:45] There's a lot of strong headwinds to uncover ideas and information that has been hidden forever,
[08:55] so it's slow.
[09:50] Interviewer: We're often asked, how can I get a functional analysis of my variant done?
[09:57] There are several paths to do that.
[09:59] In the past, we had parents contact us directly when we ran different programs
[10:04] that we were allowed to talk to parents.
[10:07] Right now, we need to shift the parents' entry point to the registries, the family foundations,
[10:14] and Grin Therapeutics has their entry point shifted to a free genetic counseling program called Informed DNA.
[10:23] That's always the starting point.
[10:25] I encourage every single parent to join the registries.
[10:28] Liz today mentioned how it can be fatiguing.
[10:32] It seems like there's so many, but the data is absolutely essential.
[10:36] That's the entry point.
